title: Supersharers of fake news on Twitter
screen_reason: Behavioural panel study of 664,391 registered US voters on Twitter during the 2020 election, reporting a concentration statistic (0.3% of the panel, 2,107 supersharers, accounted for 80% of fake news shares), a sharing prevalence (7.0% of all political news shared by the panel linked to fake news sources), a network exposure share (1.66% of political news available to the average panelist from accounts they follow linked to fake news sources) and a reach figure (5.2% of registered voters follow a supersharer). Multiple constructs with explicit denominators.

estimates.date: August to November 2020 (2020 US presidential election period)
estimates.measure_type: share of all fake news links shared by the panel that came from the top 0.3% of panelists (supersharers)
estimates.value_raw: an extremely small fraction of our sample (0.3%; only 2107 people) accounted for 80% of the tweets linking to fake news sources
estimates.conc_group_label: supersharers: the 2,107 most prolific sharers of fake news among the panel, 0.3% of 664,391 registered US voters active on Twitter
estimates.denominator: all tweets linking to fake news sources posted by a panel of 664,391 registered US voters active on Twitter from August to November 2020; the panel is registered voters matched to Twitter accounts
estimates.definition: Supersharers are defined by construction as the set of most prolific fake-news sharers accounting for 80% of fake news content shared on the platform by the panel; the 0.3% is the size of that set as a share of the panel
estimates.misinfo_def: “a source-level definition of fake news as domains that portray as legitimate news outlets but do not have the ‘editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information’”
estimates.source_quote: only 2107 people) accounted for 80% of the tweets linking to fake news sources. We label
estimates.page_loc: Results, first paragraph, p. 2 (the sentence reads “However, an extremely small fraction of our sample (0.3%; only 2107 people) accounted for 80% of the tweets linking to fake news sources.”, broken across lines in the source text); Figure 1B; Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Manually labelled list of fake news sites from Grinberg et al. (2019), updated using NewsGuard ratings; robustness to different operationalisations reported in supplementary section S3. Political tweets identified by a machine-learning classifier trained and validated against human coders
estimates.moderator_quote: We identify supersharers (N = 2107) as the most prolific sharers of fake news that account for 80% of fake news content shared on the platform.
estimates.notes: The 80% is a definitional threshold, not an estimated quantity: the supersharer group was constructed as the smallest set accounting for 80% of fake news shares, so the estimated number is the GROUP SIZE (0.3%, 2,107 people), not the share. R1 is satisfied because both sides are stated. Comparable concentration for non-fake political news is far weaker: the equivalent 80% of nonfake political news required 11,199 panelists (about 1.7%), and Figure 1B contrasts the two curves.

estimates.measure_type: % of all political news links shared by the voter panel that pointed to fake news sources, on an average day
estimates.value_raw: On an average day, 7.0% [95% confidence interval (CI): 6.7%, 7.4%] of all political news shared by the panel of 664,391 individuals linked to fake news sources
estimates.denominator: all political news links shared by the panel of 664,391 registered US voters on an average day; political tweets identified by a trained machine-learning classifier and restricted to tweets with external links
estimates.definition: Shared link resolved to a domain on the fake news source list (Grinberg et al., updated with NewsGuard)
estimates.misinfo_def: “a source-level definition of fake news as domains that portray as legitimate news outlets but do not have the ‘editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information’”
estimates.n: political news shares of 664,391 panelists (number of shares not stated)
estimates.source_quote: On an average day, 7.0% [95% confidence interval (CI): 6.7%, 7.4%] of all political news shared by the panel of 664,391 individuals
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Manually labelled fake news domain list from Grinberg et al. (2019) updated with NewsGuard ratings; political classification by an ML classifier validated against human coders
estimates.moderator_quote: To focus on political news, we restrict the analysis to tweets with external links that were identified as political by a machine learning classifier that we trained and validated against human coders.
estimates.notes: Denominator is POLITICAL news shares with external links, not all tweets, so this is not a share of everything shared. Time series collapsed to the paper's own stated representative value, the average day over August–November 2020 (Figure 1A shows the daily series, which rose after election day on election-fraud allegations). 80% of this quantity is produced by 0.3% of the panel (see the CONCENTRATION row), so it is not a typical user's behaviour.

estimates.measure_type: % of political news available to the average panelist from the accounts they follow that linked to fake news sources
estimates.value_raw: absolute rates of 4.11% versus 1.66% [the average follower of a supersharer versus the average panelist]
estimates.denominator: the political news content available to the average panelist from the accounts they follow (panel of 664,391 registered US voters; network analyses use the 641,144 panelists with complete network information)
estimates.definition: Political news links from fake news domains as a share of all political news links available to a panelist from the accounts they follow, following the content-composition approach of Grinberg et al. and González-Bailón et al.
estimates.misinfo_def: “a source-level definition of fake news as domains that portray as legitimate news outlets but do not have the ‘editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information’”
estimates.n: 664,391 panelists (network measures computed on 641,144 with complete network information)
estimates.page_loc: Results, RQ1 section, p. 2 (full sentence: “Moreover, the average follower of a supersharer was 2.5 times as likely to get political news linking to fake news sources from their network compared with the average panelist (absolute rates of 4.11% versus 1.66%).”; the quoted span starts mid-word because “absolute” is hyphenated across a line break)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same fake news domain list; content available from followed accounts computed per panelist
estimates.moderator_quote: Following the approach used in prior work (2, 4, 19), we examined the composition of content available to panelists from the accounts that they follow (see materials and methods for more details).
estimates.notes: POTENTIAL rather than realised exposure: this is the composition of what accounts a panelist follows POSTED, not what the panelist saw or clicked, so it is an upper-bound feed-composition measure. Coded exposure_type diet_share for that reason and flagged borderline. The main figure taken is the average panelist (1.66%); the 4.11% is the subgroup of supersharer followers and is kept in value_raw for reference. Note this 1.66% exposure share is well below the 7.0% sharing share, because sharing is dominated by a tiny group.

estimates.measure_type: % of registered voters on Twitter who directly follow at least one fake-news supersharer
estimates.value_raw: We found that 5.2% of registered voters on Twitter directly follow a supersharer
estimates.denominator: 641,144 panelists (registered US voters on Twitter) for whom complete network information was available
estimates.definition: Panelist directly follows at least one of the 2,107 supersharers
estimates.misinfo_def: “a source-level definition of fake news as domains that portray as legitimate news outlets but do not have the ‘editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information’”
estimates.source_quote: a sizable 5.2% of registered voters on the platform.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (“We find that supersharers are important members of the network, reaching a sizable 5.2% of registered voters on the platform.”); the same figure is given in Results RQ1 and the Discussion
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Supersharer status derived from the fake news domain list; the reach measure itself is a follower-graph relation
estimates.moderator_quote: Despite being only 0.3% of the population, supersharers reached 5.2% of registered voters in our sample and about a fifth of the heaviest consumers of fake news.
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATOR: this is reach of the ACCOUNTS, not verified reach of fake news items. Following a supersharer is a network relation; the paper does not show that these 5.2% saw a fake news post. It is recorded as REACH because the paper frames it as reach and it is behavioural, but it is flagged borderline and should not be pooled with item-level reach estimates. The denominator is also the network subsample (641,144), not the full panel (664,391).

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (1) “Supersharers accounted for nearly a quarter [24.4% (95% CI: 24.1%, 24.8%)] of the fake news available to their average follower and were the only source of fake news for 11.3% of their followers.” This is a second concentration-flavoured statistic, but its group share (0.3% of the panel) and its content share (24.4% of fake news in a follower's feed) have incommensurate denominators, so forcing it into the R1 conc_group_pct/conc_share_pct pair would be misleading. Recorded here instead; an adjudicator may want it as a supplementary concentration row. (2) “22.1% of panelists in the top decile of fake news consumption follow a supersharer”: a subgroup of the 5.2% reach row. (3) Per-capita sharing intensities: the average supersharer posted 2.8 links to fake news sources a day versus 0.1 for the heaviest nonfake sharers and 0.01 for the panel, and 15.9 versus 5.0 versus 0.3 political news links a day. These are clean verbatim per-capita intensities and could support a SHARING/per_capita_intensity row; not extracted because the 7.0% content share already represents panel-level sharing and R4 favours the cleaner measure. (4) Supersharer demographics (59% women vs 49–52% in reference groups; 64% Republican; average age 58.2; overrepresentation in Florida, Arizona and Texas; income about $2,500 higher than expected): composition of the misinformation-sharing group, not a prevalence share, and the paper's headline framing is comparative rather than a party-split prevalence. (5) “no more than 7.1% (95% CI: 2.0%, 12.2%) of supersharers can be considered as bots” and the panel's 1.2%: an automation share, not a misinformation share. (6) Retweet rates (74.7% supersharers, 59.9% heaviest nonfake sharers, 32.7% panel): behavioural, not veracity. (7) Median supersharer at the 86th percentile of network influence, 29% above the median nonfake supersharer: an influence statistic. (8) “3.4% of Americans on Twitter followed an account controlled by Russia's foreign influence campaign in 2016” and the $435 million digital ad spend: figures cited from other publications, barred by R8. (9) Group sizes of the reference sets (SS-NF N = 11,199; average fake news sharers N = 10,464): design parameters. Note that N = 11,199 out of 664,391 implies the 80% concentration threshold for NONFAKE political news falls at about 1.7% of panelists, but that percentage is not stated in the paper, so it is not recorded as a value.

rob.design: Behavioural panel study. 664,391 registered US voters matched to Twitter accounts and active during the 2020 US presidential election (August to November 2020); network analyses use the 641,144 panelists with complete network information. Fake news defined at source level using the manually labelled domain list of Grinberg et al. (2019) updated with NewsGuard ratings, with robustness checks across operationalisations (S3), supersharer thresholds (S5), outliers (S6) and matched-sample specifications (S12). Political content identified by a machine-learning classifier trained and validated against human coders; no accuracy statistic for the classifier is given in the main text. Automation checked three ways (Botometer plus manual labelling, posting-time patterns, app metadata). Confidence intervals reported for the key shares. Stated limitations: the voter-record-matched sample may differ systematically from the full population, particularly excluding eligible but unregistered voters; supersharing on platforms other than Twitter is unknown; Twitter's user base has since changed. Ethics approval from Ben-Gurion University (SISE-2022-30); data on Dryad with restricted-access components on request.
rob.item6_quote: Similar to prior work (4, 6), we rely on a source-level definition of fake news as domains that portray as legitimate news outlets but do not have the “editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information” (17). We rely on the manually labeled list of fake news sites by Grinberg et al. (4), updated using NewsGuard ratings
rob.item10_quote: On an average day, 7.0% [95% confidence interval (CI): 6.7%, 7.4%] of all political news shared by the panel of 664,391 individuals linked to fake news sources. However, an extremely small fraction of our sample (0.3%; only 2107 people) accounted for 80% of the tweets linking to fake news sources.
